bp: Digital advertising is not only about finding a likely buyer. It is also about deciding where a brand should not appear. A family-friendly company may be willing to advertise beside a romance story, but not beside a chapter that contains graphic violence, self-harm, hate, or another category that damages trust. On large story platforms, a human reviewer cannot read every chapter before every ad decision. This paper serves that practical screening problem: given narrative fiction from Wattpad, decide whether a story chapter carries one of nine standard safety risks. The paper matters because brand safety in fiction is different from spotting a single banned word. The risky signal may be spread across plot, tone, implication, and repeated scenes. The authors therefore build a dedicated text dataset of 51 stories and 435 chapters, then compare general language models used without task examples against models trained on these labels.
wh: The hard part is that brand safety is a judgment about meaning, not just vocabulary. A chapter can contain explicit wording that clearly points to a safety category, and a broad language model may catch that. But the abstract says the difficult cases are nuanced safety concerns, where the risk depends on context. A violent word might be harmless in metaphor, while a seemingly ordinary scene may imply substance use, abuse, or other unsafe associations. The advertising system also faces a cost imbalance: a missed unsafe chapter can hurt reputation, while too many false alarms can remove acceptable inventory and reduce advertising effectiveness. Existing solutions are described as limited because the field lacks comprehensive datasets and systematic comparisons for this exact task. Without shared labeled examples, it is difficult to know whether a detector has learned brand safety or has merely learned familiar wording from other text tasks.
naive: A smart beginner would start with two simple checks. First, make a list of risky words and block chapters that contain them. Second, ask a general language model to read the chapter and label it by category, without giving it specialized training examples. Both are plausible because some unsafe content is explicit. They fail for the same reason: the detector must understand how words behave inside a story. Keyword lists miss implied scenes and overreact to harmless mentions. A general model may know broad safety concepts, but the paper reports that such zero-example use struggles with nuanced concerns. Brand safety needs category-specific evidence from the target kind of text.
ap: The paper's central move is to turn brand-safety detection from an open-ended judgment into a measured text classification problem with task-specific evidence. The authors first create a dataset built for this purpose: narrative fiction from Wattpad, organized as 51 stories and 435 chapters, labeled across nine standard safety categories. That dataset gives the system concrete examples of what counts as safe or unsafe in this domain. They then compare two styles of automation. One style asks large general models, including ChatGPT and GPT-3, to infer labels directly from instructions. The other style adjusts models, including RoBERTa and GPT-3, on the labeled examples before testing them. The core finding is mechanical rather than magical: broad language knowledge helps on explicit categories, but specialized training data teaches the detector the recurring signals that matter for this brand-safety setting.
mech: The mechanism begins with a chapter of narrative fiction. The chapter is treated as text to be judged against nine safety categories, not as a single overall bad-or-good label. Human annotation supplies the reference decisions for the dataset: for each chapter, the data records which categories apply. Once that evidence exists, the paper runs comparative detection paths. In the zero-example path, a general language model receives the text and category instructions, then produces a safety judgment without having been trained on these Wattpad labels. This tests how far broad prior language knowledge can go. In the trained path, a model is shown labeled examples first. During training, it changes its internal scoring rules so that chapters with similar wording, context, and narrative cues receive similar category decisions. At evaluation time, each model reads held-out chapter text, scores the possible safety categories, and outputs predicted labels. The predictions are compared with the annotations to reveal which approach is reliable and which categories remain difficult. The paper reports that zero-example methods show promise for explicit content categories, while trained models do better overall, with RoBERTa maintaining strong performance. The output is therefore not just a detector, but evidence about when general language models are enough and when task-specific training is needed.
math: The main mathematical idea is supervised classification: learn a rule that maps an input text to one or more category decisions by studying examples whose answers are already known. In everyday terms, the model is learning where to draw boundaries between chapters that do and do not fit each safety category. The boundary is not a hand-written line like "contains this word." It is a learned scoring rule built from many small textual clues. Fine-tuning means taking a model that already knows general language patterns and adjusting it with the brand-safety labels so its scores become better aligned with this task. The comparison with zero-example inference is also a measurement idea. The paper asks whether broad language knowledge alone is enough, or whether repeated labeled cases reduce error. Probability is present in the background because each category decision is uncertain: the model scores how strongly the text resembles examples of that risk, and the evaluation checks whether those scores match human labels. The tradeoff is generality versus specialization. A general model can handle many tasks without new labels, but specialized training can better capture category-specific patterns. The risk is that the learned boundary may reflect the dataset's 51 stories and 435 chapters more than all narrative fiction.
dots: This paper sits in three repo-level neighborhoods. In the advertising and e-commerce family, it belongs to the trust branch: commercial systems must decide not only what to show, rank, or bid on, but also what associations are unsafe for brands and users. It is close to unsafe advertising and scam-detection work because all of them replace a flat marketplace score with a safety judgment under incomplete evidence. In the language-model family, it tests a recurring 2026 question: when can a broad language model be used directly, and when does a narrower trained model beat it because the task has local rules? In the text-mining family, it is a document classification problem, but the documents are long narrative chapters rather than short posts or clean product descriptions. The paper also touches recurring ideas of similarity, probability, and ranking: chapters are compared to labeled examples, category chances are estimated, and content may later be allowed, reviewed, or suppressed.
ww: The approach works better than the naive one because it gives the detector the right kind of experience. Brand safety in narrative fiction depends on repeated patterns: how a scene is described, whether an act is central or incidental, whether a category is explicit or implied, and how chapter-level context changes the reading. A keyword rule throws away most of that structure. A general model used without examples may understand broad language but still lack the operational boundary that advertisers need for the nine categories. Labeled chapters supply that boundary. When a trained model sees many annotated cases, it can learn that some word patterns are weak evidence, some combinations are stronger, and some categories are harder because the signal is indirect. The abstract's result matches this reasoning: zero-example approaches are promising on explicit content, where the surface clue is obvious, but they struggle with nuanced safety concerns. Fine-tuned models, especially RoBERTa, improve because they are fitted to the actual decision standard instead of guessing the standard from general knowledge.
po: The payoff is a usable research resource and a clearer implementation lesson for automated brand safety. The dataset gives researchers 51 Wattpad stories, 435 chapters, and labels across nine standard safety categories, which makes systematic comparison possible. The experiments show that general language models can help with explicit categories, but reliable detection needs specialized training data for subtle cases. For platforms and advertisers, the practical result is guidance: do not treat a general model prompt as a complete safety system. Use labeled examples, evaluate by category, and expect different risk categories to have different failure patterns.
limits: The abstract does not prove that the detector will work across all fiction platforms, languages, genres, advertisers, or policy definitions. The dataset is valuable but still bounded: 51 stories and 435 chapters from Wattpad. Human annotations define the target, so unclear or disputed safety standards will affect the learned labels. Fine-tuned models may also learn patterns specific to this collection. The paper reports comparative performance and category-specific challenges, but the abstract does not establish deployment behavior under changing policies, adversarial writing, or real advertising review workflows.
